synopsis: Bayesian analysis can formally combine simulation-derived prior evidence with physical tests, potentially reducing physical testing, but the corpus gives no fixed virtual-to-physical exchange rate: this depends on assessor acceptance of prior strength and documented simulation/toolchain credibility [f6898, f14218, f14227, f14275]. Prior sensitivity is substantial: the cited independent, on-road ISSRE 2019 analysis reduced RAND’s 275 million fatality-free miles to 69 million with a strong prior carrying 90% prior confidence, but increased it to 476 million with a weak prior; proponents and critics therefore disagree about simulation-derived priors’ benefits [f6900, f6901, f6902, f7437]. The recommendations are to use conservative Bayesian methods because assessors will challenge priors, and to learn machine-response distributions from existing machines before 2027, even where brake hardware differs [f6899, f14222, f6405]. Bayesian or hierarchical pooling can share evidence across genuinely similar machine families while retaining variant uncertainty, but requires a justified similarity model to avoid hiding a bad variant [f645, f646]. Sequential testing permits early stopping when evidence is clearly good or bad, provided acceptance thresholds, statistical tests and stopping rules are fixed in advance—not chosen when results look favorable [f643, f644, f6903, f6905, f14225]. Its use in the four-month validation window is attractive, although the chapter labels that application expert opinion while the glossary presents trial savings and program attractiveness as a finding [f6904, f14224].

relations.note: Both report 90% prior confidence reducing 275 million miles to 69 million.
Both report a weak prior increasing required miles from 275 million to 476 million.
Both recommend conservative Bayesian methods because priors will face assessor challenges.
Both describe disagreement over simulation priors; the chapter adds the numerical range.
Both require predetermined stopping rules; the glossary explains invalid opportunistic stopping.
Both describe SPRT early stopping; the glossary specifies checks after each trial or batch.
SPRT supplies a specific sequential method for threshold-based early stopping.
General sequential requirements specify acceptance thresholds and statistical tests alongside predetermined stopping rules.
The glossary illustrates simulation priors updated by hundreds of physical trials.
Using simulation as prior evidence requires documented simulation credibility.
Established updating methods do not establish an assessor-independent virtual-to-physical exchange rate.
The road-testing study provides evidence for the glossary’s warning about prior sensitivity.
The strong-prior result supplies the lower end of the disputed mileage range.
The weak-prior result supplies the upper end and illustrates sensitivity.
Sharing information across variants requires justified similarity to avoid masking a bad variant.
Existing-machine measurements offer a concrete source of prior evidence for Bayesian updating.
Early stopping motivates the proposed use within the four-month validation window.
Both describe four-month-window attractiveness, but label its evidential status differently.
